# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a form of de novo systolic heart failure that emerges toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery in previously healthy women. It is a potentially life-threatening heart disease that emerges towards the end of pregnancy or in the first months postpartum in previously healthy women, with symptoms and signs similar to those of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy. [1] Despite considerable research, diagnosis is frequently delayed and the condition remains associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. PPCM is a type of de novo heart failure occurring in pregnant women in the late stages of pregnancy or following delivery, and despite extensive research, diagnosing and managing it remains challenging, resulting in significant morbidity and mortality. [2]

## Definition and Diagnosis

The first universally accepted definition arose from a National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) and Office of Rare Diseases workshop. PPCM is a rare life-threatening cardiomyopathy of unknown cause occurring in the peripartum period in previously healthy women; in April 1997 the NHLBI and the Office of Rare Diseases convened a workshop to foster systematic review and develop recommendations. [3] These criteria require heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, no recognizable heart disease before the last month of pregnancy, and echocardiographic left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction. [3] The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) subsequently refined the definition. The diagnosis is based on three criteria from the 2010 ESC Working Group definition: development of heart failure toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, and LV systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction generally below 45%. [4] Diagnosis is essentially one of exclusion and requires echocardiographic confirmation. Echocardiography showing decreased myocardial function is essential for the diagnosis. [5] Because the symptoms overlap with normal late pregnancy, recognition is often delayed. Symptoms of heart failure mimic those of normal pregnancy, often resulting in a delay in diagnosis and preventable complications. [5] Natriuretic peptides and cardiac MRI support diagnosis and risk stratification. [6]

## Epidemiology and Risk Factors

The true incidence is unknown and varies markedly geographically. The incidence varies geographically, most likely because of socioeconomic and genetic factors. [1] In the United States, estimates approximate 1 in 2000 to 1 in 4000 live births, while rates are higher in parts of Africa. PPCM occurs in approximately 1:2000 deliveries in the United States and worldwide. [7] Identified risk factors include African ancestry, advanced maternal age, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and multiple gestation. Incidence is higher in African-American women and in women with older maternal age, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and multiple gestation pregnancies. [5] An early US cohort characterized the typical clinical profile and associated conditions. Data from 123 women with cardiomyopathy diagnosed during or after pregnancy showed PPCM patients had a mean age of 31 years and common associated conditions were gestational hypertension, tocolytic therapy, and twin pregnancy. [8]

## Pathophysiology

A major advance was the recognition of an oxidative-stress–driven hormonal mechanism. In a landmark study, female mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of *stat3* develop PPCM, with enhanced cardiac cathepsin D activity associated with generation of a cleaved antiangiogenic and proapoptotic 16-kDa form of the nursing hormone prolactin. [9] Treatment with bromocriptine prevented the development of PPCM, whereas forced myocardial generation of 16-kDa prolactin impaired the cardiac capillary network and function, recapitulating the phenotype. [9] This 16-kDa fragment acts as a key pathological mediator. The hypothesis holds that an antiangiogenic 16-kDa prolactin fragment, enzymatically generated by cathepsin D, impairs myocardial microvascularization, with excessive generation possibly due to high prolactin secretion near term and an enhanced oxidative microenvironment. [10] The fragment damages cardiomyocytes downstream. The 16-kDa prolactin, a product of oxidative stress, damages cardiomyocytes through microRNA-146a and the NF-κB pathway. [11] An antiangiogenic milieu, including elevated soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), links PPCM to preeclampsia. Elevated levels of vascular endothelial growth factor, sFlt-1, and placental hormones—common in preeclampsia and multiple gestations—have been associated with the pathogenesis of PPCM. [11]

A genetic predisposition is now well established. In 172 women with PPCM, 43 dilated-cardiomyopathy genes were sequenced; the prevalence of truncating variants (15%) was significantly higher than in a reference population (4.7%), with two-thirds in *TTN*, encoding titin. [12] In a well-characterized cohort of 83 women, the presence of TTN truncating variants was significantly correlated with a lower ejection fraction at 1-year follow-up. [12] Earlier family studies first connected the two disorders. Titin gene mutations are common in families with both peripartum cardiomyopathy and dilated cardiomyopathy. [13] Subsequent reviews have synthesized these risk factors and mechanisms. [14]

## Management

Standard heart-failure therapy is the foundation of treatment, with adjustments for pregnancy and lactation. Medical management is similar to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction of other etiologies, but adjustments during pregnancy are necessary to ensure fetal safety. [5] The ESC Heart Failure Association has published comprehensive position statements guiding diagnosis and management. [15][16] Disease-specific therapy with the prolactin-release inhibitor bromocriptine has been studied prospectively. An anti-angiogenic cleaved prolactin fragment is considered causal for PPCM, and in a randomized study bromocriptine treatment was associated with a high rate of full LV recovery and low morbidity and mortality compared with cohorts not treated with bromocriptine. [17] However, the trial lacked a non-treated control arm, and the evidence base remains limited. A critical unanswered question concerns the use of bromocriptine in addition to guideline therapy, and the trial had no non-use control group, leaving many unanswered questions. [18] The rationale and design of that trial reflect the prolactin hypothesis. [19] Meta-analyses suggest a possible benefit on LV recovery but emphasize the need for adequately powered trials. [20] Worldwide registries have characterized presentation and management across regions. The EURObservational Research Programme allows comparison of women from around the world, of different ethnic backgrounds, presenting with PPCM, reporting 6- and 12-month outcomes. [21][22]

## Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancy

Outcomes are heterogeneous, ranging from full recovery to chronic heart failure, transplantation, or death. In the IPAC study, event-free survival at 1 year was 93%, transplant-free survival was 95%, and at 12 months 72% of patients achieved an LVEF ≥50%. [23] While 50% of women experience dramatic myocardial recovery, others develop chronic cardiomyopathy and progress toward poorer outcomes including death or cardiac transplantation. [24] A GNB3 polymorphism has been associated with recovery, illustrating ongoing efforts at risk stratification. [25] Many patients recover within months. Despite a mortality rate of up to 10% and a high risk of relapse in subsequent pregnancies, many patients recover within 3 to 6 months of disease onset. [26] Subsequent pregnancy carries significant risk, particularly with incomplete recovery. PPCM is a rare and sometimes fatal form of heart failure, and little is known about the outcomes of subsequent pregnancies in women who have had the disorder. [27] Biomarker research continues to seek diagnostic and prognostic tools. [28] Contemporary reviews underscore persisting global inequities in access and outcomes. [29][30]

## Conclusion

PPCM is a distinct, potentially reversible cause of pregnancy-associated heart failure with an emerging vascular-hormonal and genetic pathophysiology. Standard heart-failure therapy remains central, while bromocriptine offers a promising disease-specific approach requiring further trial validation. Early recognition, multidisciplinary care, and careful counseling regarding future pregnancies are essential to improving outcomes.
